meta.title: Road markings
meta.summary: You will understand which lines you may cross and when, what the yellow markings and transverse markings mean, what the arrows on lanes show, and where markings mean you cannot stop.

lesson.h: What road markings are and what colour they are
p: Horizontal markings are lines, arrows, inscriptions and other signs on the carriageway. They set specific traffic modes and procedures, so their requirements are as binding as the requirements of signs ⟦14⟧.

Markings are white or yellow. Lines 1.4 (no stopping), 1.10 (no parking) and 1.17 (route vehicle stops and taxi ranks) are always yellow. The 1.28 grid, which marks the controlled area of an intersection, is also yellow. Remember: a yellow line at the edge of the road almost always relates to stopping or parking.

Vertical markings (2.1-2.7) are applied to road structures: the piers of bridges and flyovers, bollards on islands, guide posts, barriers and kerbs on hazardous sections. They help you notice an obstruction in time.
lesson.tip: Marking numbers start with 1 for horizontal markings and with 2 for vertical markings.

lesson.h: Solid lines 1.1, 1.2, 1.3: you must not cross
p: Crossing lines 1.1-1.3 is prohibited. There are exceptions for only two of them: you may cross 1.1 and 1.2 to stop on the shoulder, and you may cross 1.1 as an exception when driving around an obstruction, if there is no other way round it. There are no such exceptions for the double solid line 1.3.

On a two-lane road where line 1.1 and (or) sign 3.20 separates the oncoming traffic flows, driving onto the oncoming side is prohibited, except in cases provided for by the Rules ⟦15⟧. On a motorway, in the event of a forced stop, the vehicle is moved to the right of the line marking the edge of the carriageway ⟦16⟧.

A solid line also affects stopping: you must not stop if less than 3 m would remain between your car and the solid marking line (other than the line marking the edge of the carriageway) and this would obstruct traffic ⟦17⟧.
list: 1.1 (solid line) separates oncoming traffic flows and marks lane boundaries in hazardous places, marks the boundaries of carriageway areas where entry is prohibited, the boundaries of parking spaces, and the edge of the carriageway on ordinary roads.
1.2 (wide solid line) marks the edge of the carriageway on motorways.
1.3 (double solid line) separates oncoming traffic flows on roads with four lanes or more.
lesson.tip: You do not cross a double solid line even to turn into a yard or to make a U-turn.

p: Lines 1.5-1.8 may be crossed from either side. But remember: permission to cross a line does not override other rules, for example the prohibitions on overtaking.

On an acceleration lane you build up speed and then change onto the adjacent lane, giving way to those already travelling on the road. Before an exit, change lane onto the deceleration lane in good time and reduce speed only there ⟦18⟧.
list: 1.5 separates oncoming traffic flows on roads with two or three lanes and marks lane boundaries where there are two or more lanes in one direction.
1.6 is the approach line: a broken line whose dashes are roughly 3 times longer than the gaps. It warns that solid line 1.1 or 1.11 will begin shortly.
1.7 (short dashes with equal gaps) marks lanes within an intersection.
1.8 (wide broken line) separates an acceleration or deceleration lane from the main lane.
lesson.tip: If you see during overtaking that the dashes have become long (1.6), finish the manoeuvre and return to your lane.

p: 1.11 consists of a solid line and a broken line side by side. It is applied where changing lane is allowed only from one of the lanes, and also at places for U-turns and for entering or leaving parking areas. You may cross 1.11 from the side of the broken line. From the side of the solid line, only when completing an overtaking manoeuvre or driving around an obstruction.

1.9 marks the boundaries of reversible lanes, where the direction of travel can change, and separates oncoming traffic flows when the lane-control signals are off. If there are no lane-control signals or they are switched off, the line may be crossed when it is to the driver's right. When the lane-control signals are on, it may be crossed from either side if it separates lanes running in the same direction.

When the lane-control signals are switched off, you must immediately change lane to the right, beyond line 1.9. Crossing line 1.9 where it separates oncoming traffic flows is prohibited while the lane-control signals are off. Entering a lane marked on both sides by lines 1.9 is prohibited while the lane-control signal above it is switched off ⟦19⟧.
lesson.tip: At line 1.11, look at the side nearer to you: broken - you may cross; solid - only to return after overtaking or driving around an obstruction.

lesson.h: Transverse markings: where to stop and where to give way
list: 1.12 (stop line) marks the place where a driver stops at sign 2.5 or at a prohibitory traffic light (or traffic controller) signal. Sign 5.33 may be used in its place ⟦20⟧.
1.13 marks a place where, if necessary, you must stop, giving way to traffic on the intersecting road.
1.20 warns that you are approaching marking 1.13.
1.21 (the word “STOP”) warns that you are approaching stop line 1.12, where it is used together with sign 2.5.
lesson.tip: You do not drive over the stop line: the car stops before it, not on top of it.

p: At an uncontrolled crossing, give way to pedestrians who are crossing the carriageway in your direction of travel ⟦21⟧. If a vehicle in the adjacent lane has stopped or slowed down in front of the crossing, you may drive on only after making sure there are no pedestrians in front of it ⟦22⟧.

A pedestrian crossing is marked with signs 5.16.1-5.16.3 and (or) marking 1.14.1-1.14.3 ⟦23⟧: a “zebra crossing” on its own is enough. Stopping on the crossing and less than 5 m before it is prohibited ⟦24⟧, and making a U-turn on it is not allowed either ⟦25⟧.
list: 1.14.1 and 1.14.2 (a “zebra crossing”) mark an uncontrolled pedestrian crossing; the arrows of 1.14.2 show the direction pedestrians walk.
1.14.3 marks a pedestrian crossing where traffic is controlled by traffic lights.
1.15 marks the place where a cycle track crosses the carriageway.

1.18 is lane arrows: they show which directions are allowed at the intersection from that lane. It is used on its own or together with signs 5.8.1, 5.8.2. An arrow allowing a left turn from the far left lane also allows a U-turn from it. An arrow showing a dead end means that turning into the nearest carriageway is prohibited.

1.16.1-1.16.3 mark traffic islands: 1.16.1 where oncoming flows are divided, 1.16.2 where flows in one direction are divided, 1.16.3 where flows merge. Islands, bollards and supports in the middle of the road are passed on the right, unless signs or markings require otherwise ⟦26⟧.
1.19 (warning arrows) indicates that you are approaching a narrowing of the carriageway or lines 1.1 and 1.11.
lesson.tip: If arrow 1.18 shows only ahead, you cannot turn from that lane, even if the intersection is clear.

list: 1.4 (yellow solid line) - stopping is prohibited here. It is applied at the edge of the carriageway or along the top of the kerb, on its own or together with sign 3.27. It does not apply to route vehicles.

1.10 (yellow broken line) - parking is prohibited here, but you may stop. It is used on its own or with signs 3.28-3.30. It does not apply to taxis with the meter running, or to vehicles driven by, or carrying, people with group I or II disability or group III disability with musculoskeletal impairments.
1.17 (yellow zigzag line) - a route vehicle stop or taxi rank. Only category M2 and M3 vehicles may stop at the stopping area and within 15 m of it ⟦27⟧.
1.22 - the road (route) number.

1.23 (the letter “A”) - a lane for route vehicles, other public transport (which includes taxis) and other category M3 vehicles. No one else may drive or stop on it, even where it is separated by a broken line ⟦28⟧. The exception is cyclists and e-scooter riders in the cases set out in para. 166 and 168-1.
1.28 (yellow grid) - the controlled area of an intersection. If there is a traffic jam beyond the intersection, you must not enter it ⟦29⟧.

lesson.h: When markings and other signals disagree
list: You must follow the traffic controller's signals, even if they conflict with traffic lights, signs or markings ⟦30⟧.
If the meanings of signs, including temporary ones, and marking lines conflict with each other, or the markings are hard to see (for example, under snow), you are guided by the signs ⟦31⟧.

At road works and places with a temporary change to traffic, temporary signs on a yellow background are put up ⟦32⟧. If a temporary sign conflicts with a permanent one, the temporary sign is followed ⟦33⟧.
Markings and signs often duplicate each other: a crossing - signs 5.16.1-5.16.3 and (or) marking 1.14.1-1.14.3 ⟦34⟧; stop line 1.12 - sign 5.33 ⟦35⟧.
lesson.tip: In winter, when markings are covered with snow, look at the signs: they take priority.

list: Less than 3 m between the car and a solid line (other than the line marking the edge of the carriageway), if this obstructs traffic ⟦36⟧.
On a pedestrian crossing and within 5 m before it ⟦37⟧.
At a stopping area marked with marking 1.17, and within 15 m of it, except for category M2 and M3 vehicles ⟦38⟧.
Within 30 m of the edge of the intersecting carriageway, except on the side opposite a side approach of a T-junction with a solid line or a central reservation ⟦39⟧.
At yellow solid line 1.4 you cannot stop; at yellow broken line 1.10 you cannot leave the car parked.
lesson.tip: Stopping means up to 5 minutes, or longer if needed for boarding, alighting, loading or unloading. If you stay longer than 5 minutes for any other reason, that is parking.

keyFacts: You may cross 1.1 and 1.2 to stop on the shoulder, and 1.1 when driving around an obstruction if there is no other way round it ⟦2⟧
Lines 1.5-1.8 may be crossed from either side ⟦3⟧
1.11 is crossed from the side of the broken line; from the side of the solid line, only when completing overtaking or driving around an obstruction ⟦4⟧
1.3 separates oncoming flows on roads with 4 or more lanes; 1.5 on roads with 2 or 3 lanes ⟦5⟧
Yellow lines: 1.4 - no stopping, 1.10 - no parking, 1.17 - route vehicle stops and taxi ranks ⟦6⟧
1.12 is the stopping place at sign 2.5 or a prohibitory traffic light signal ⟦7⟧
Arrow 1.18 allowing a left turn from the far left lane also allows a U-turn ⟦8⟧
Stopping is prohibited on a crossing and within 5 m before it, and also if less than 3 m remains before a solid line and this obstructs traffic ⟦9⟧
The traffic controller's signals take priority over markings ⟦10⟧
If signs (including temporary ones) and marking lines conflict, or the markings are hard to see, the signs are followed ⟦11⟧
Route vehicles, other public transport including taxis, and category M3 vehicles use the lane marked with the letter “A” (1.23) ⟦12⟧
mistakes: Crossing the double solid line to turn into a yard. Line 1.3 must not be crossed; there are no exceptions for it.
Confusing 1.4 and 1.10: the yellow solid line prohibits stopping, while the yellow broken line prohibits only parking.
Not noticing the approach line 1.6 and starting to overtake just before a solid line. Long dashes are a signal to finish the manoeuvre.
Crossing 1.11 from the side of the solid line to start overtaking. From the side of the solid line, it may be crossed only when completing overtaking or driving around an obstruction.
Stopping on the stop line or beyond it. You must stop before line 1.12.
Thinking that markings take priority over signs. Where signs, including temporary ones, conflict with markings, the signs are followed ⟦13⟧.
